questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presented with lower abdominal pain and bleeding between menstrual periods. She also reported intermittent fevers to 101°F (38.3°C). She had appendicitis age 13 years and had no known drug allergies. She had had unprotected vaginal intercourse with two casual male partners in the past 3 months. On examination, her temperature was 101.2°F (38.4°C), blood pressure 124/82 mmHg, pulse 80/minute, and respiratory rate of 14 breaths/minute, SaO2 98% on room air. A mucopurulent discharge was visible over the cervix, there was cervical motion and adnexal tenderness, and the cervix os bled easily upon application of pressure. NAAT studies were sent for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric treatment?

options.text: Azithromycin 1 gram orally for one dose
Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM for one dose
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BID
Metronidazole 2 gram orally for one dose
Metronidazole 500 mg orally BID for 7 days

questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BID In patient with the above clinical constellation, a low threshold to treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease should be maintained. Empiric outpatient therapy should cover Gonorrhea, Chlamydia, and anaerobic organisms. Current recommendations are to initiate therapy with one dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours with follow-up in 3 days for repeat evaluation. Other therapeutic regimens would not adequately cover likely culprit organisms.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q21

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman was 40+2 weeks pregnant. She had a prolonged membrane rupture with multiple vaginal examinations. On exam, her temperature was 39.2°C, and her heart rate was 118 beats/minute. Purulent amniotic fluid was noted.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Ureaplasma urealyticum Chorioamnionitis is usually an ascending polymicrobial infection. All of the options have been implicated in the pathogenesis of chorioamnionitis. However, the most common causative organism is Ureaplasma urealyticum, which causes 47% of cases.

questions.model_answer: In a sexually active young woman or a woman at risk for sexually transmitted infection with no other explanation: (1) lower abdominal/pelvic pain with pelvic organ tenderness on bimanual examination, with or without cervical motion tenderness; (2) uterine or adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination; (3) mucopurulent cervical discharge or white blood cells in the vaginal secretions on microscopy (supportive: oral temperature >38C, raised ESR/CRP, documented gonococcal or chlamydial cervicitis).

questions.question: Pelvic inflammatory disease.

parts.text: What are two short-term complications of PID?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 short-term complications of PID?

questions.model_answer: (1) Tubo-ovarian abscess (which may leak or rupture, requiring urgent surgery). (2) Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome); pelvic peritonitis is an alternative acceptable answer. Long-term sequelae - infertility, ectopic pregnancy, pelvic adhesions, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain.
questions.beyond_mandell: Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis) is not described in this chapter section; it is covered in the Mandell chlamydia/gonorrhea chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh Curtis Syndrome); Tubo-ovarian abscess. (Long term complications: hydrosalpinx, chronic pelvic pain, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, two-fold increase risk of ovarian cancer)

questions.question: Pelvic inflammatory disease.

parts.text: What are three organisms implicated in PID?

parts_raw.text: What are 3 organisms implicated in PID?

questions.model_answer: (1) Neisseria gonorrhoeae. (2) Chlamydia trachomatis. (3) Bacterial vaginosis-associated anaerobes (e.g. Prevotella, Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus) - also genital mycoplasmas, gram-negative facultative rods, streptococci, and uncommonly Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pyogenes and Histoplasma capsulatum.

cohort_answer.text: Sexually transmitted: Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, HSV, Trichomonas vaginalis (rare). Endogenous: genital-tract mycoplasmas (Mycoplasma genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum). Anaerobic: Bacteroides spp., Peptostreptococcus spp., Prevotella spp. Facultative: E. coli, Gardnerella vaginalis, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus spp.

parts_raw.text: What is the diagnosis?
What do you recommend the gynecologist immediately do?
What is the initial treatment? Name the drug and route.
What is the duration of the treatment?
If a woman with an IUD has the same gram stain but is asymptomatic, what should be done?

questions.model_answer:
a) IUD-associated pelvic inflammatory disease with a tubo-ovarian abscess/pelvic mass due to pelvic actinomycosis (branching, beaded gram-positive bacilli).
b) Remove the IUD (send it for culture) and obtain the mass for diagnosis and source control - drainage/aspiration under ultrasound or CT guidance by interventional radiology, or operative drainage/laparoscopy, with material sent for aerobic and anaerobic culture; hospitalize for parenteral broad-spectrum therapy.
c) Intravenous penicillin G (18-24 million units/day, divided q4h) - or IV ampicillin - as the anti-actinomycosis agent, given as part of broad-spectrum parenteral coverage of gonococcus, chlamydia, anaerobes and gram-negative facultative organisms (e.g. ampicillin + clindamycin + gentamicin, with doxycycline for chlamydia).
d) Parenteral therapy for about 2-6 weeks, then oral penicillin V or amoxicillin to complete 6-12 months total for pelvic actinomycosis (drainage may shorten this); the PID/anaerobic component needs 14 days of doxycycline +/- metronidazole.
e) Nothing beyond counselling and observation - Actinomyces-like organisms are seen on Pap smears in 4%-8% of IUD users, their presence has not been equated with pelvic actinomycosis, and removal of the IUD is not necessary in an asymptomatic colonized woman; advise her to report pelvic pain, fever or discharge.
questions.beyond_mandell: Actinomycosis drug, route and 6-12 month duration come from the Mandell Actinomyces chapter/standard practice, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian abscess, possibly pelvic actinomycosis pending culture. Immediate: Remove the IUD, surgical removal of mass vs IR aspirate with culture. Initial treatment: Empiric CRO 1g IV daily + doxycycline 100mg BID + metronidazole 500mg BID until well enough for oral stepdown, then metro/doxy for 14 days total, plus actino treatment (amoxil or penicillin, technically IV for 14 days then PO stepdown); actino specific: IV PenG x2 weeks then 6-12 months PO. Asymptomatic: counsel and monitor for symptoms, IUD stays in.

questions.model_answer:
a) Pelvic actinomycosis - IUD-associated chronic endometritis/PID with a tubo-ovarian (adnexal) mass.
b) Remove the IUD and send it for culture, and obtain/drain the adnexal mass (image-guided percutaneous or transvaginal drainage, or laparoscopic/operative drainage) with aerobic and anaerobic cultures; admit for parenteral therapy.
c) Intravenous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day divided q4h (or IV ampicillin 2 g q4h) for Actinomyces, within a broad-spectrum parenteral regimen also covering anaerobes, gram-negative facultative organisms, gonococcus and chlamydia (e.g. ampicillin + clindamycin + gentamicin, plus doxycycline).
d) 2-6 weeks IV, then oral penicillin V/amoxicillin to complete 6-12 months, guided by clinical and radiologic resolution; the concomitant PID regimen (doxycycline +/- metronidazole) runs 14 days.
e) Observe - Actinomyces-like organisms on Pap smear occur in 4%-8% of IUD users, do not equate with pelvic actinomycosis, and IUD removal and antibiotics are not required in an asymptomatic woman; counsel about symptoms.
questions.beyond_mandell: Penicillin dosing and the 6-12 month duration for actinomycosis are from the Mandell Actinomyces chapter/standard practice.

questions.model_answer: a) IUCD-associated pelvic actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii). b) Remove the intrauterine contraceptive device and image the pelvis (US/CT) to look for a tubo-ovarian abscess or mass. c) Intravenous penicillin G (ampicillin/penicillin G IV). d) Detection of Actinomyces-like organisms on Pap without symptoms has a low positive predictive value for pelvic infection — do NOT remove the IUCD; provide patient education and close follow-up (remove only if symptoms cannot be attributed to another cause, or if an equally suitable alternative contraception can be agreed on).

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Actinomyces israelii infection. Immediate action: Remove IUD, do pelvic US looking for abscess. Antibiotic: Ampicillin or Pen G (IV). Asymptomatic with ALOs: Part of normal flora - removal of IUD unnecessary unless causing disease (ALOs seen in ~7% of Pap smears in IUCD users; low PPV for pelvic infection; warrants patient education and follow-up, not removal, unless equally suitable contraception can be agreed on).

questions.model_answer: a) IUCD-associated pelvic actinomycosis with tubo-ovarian involvement. b) Remove the IUCD and obtain pelvic imaging (CT/MRI); drain any significant purulent collection/abscess. c) High-dose IV penicillin G (18–24 million units/day) as initial therapy, followed by oral penicillin or amoxicillin. d) For this bulky/tissue-invasive disease: 2–6 weeks parenteral therapy then oral therapy to a total of 6–12 months, extended beyond radiographic resolution to minimize relapse (a 14-day penicillin or tetracycline course suffices only for possible early actinomycotic endometritis). e) Asymptomatic Actinomyces-like organisms on Pap have low predictive value — do not remove the IUCD; provide patient education and close follow-up.

questions.model_answer: a) IUCD-associated pelvic actinomycosis with a tubo-ovarian/adnexal mass (branching/filamentous gram-positive rods with an IUCD); clue cells indicate concurrent bacterial vaginosis. b) Remove the IUCD and image/drain the adnexal collection. c) High-dose IV penicillin G. d) 2–6 weeks IV then oral penicillin/amoxicillin to a total of 6–12 months for this bulky disease. e) If uncomplicated (early actinomycotic endometritis without abscess): a 14-day course of a penicillin or a tetracycline.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer frames this as PID/bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella) with STI-oriented PID regimens; given the actinomycosis chapter, an IUCD, and branching gram-positive rods with an adnexal mass, the primary diagnosis is pelvic actinomycosis (BV/clue cells being a concurrent finding), so the regimen is high-dose penicillin, not empiric PID therapy.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian complex/abscess (polymicrobial, often including Gardnerella); clue cells suggest BV, particularly Gardnerella vaginalis. Immediate action: Beta-HCG to rule out ectopic pregnancy; Chlamydia + gonorrhoeae NAAT prior to Rx, screen for other STIs including HIV; empiric Rx. Abx route/regimen: Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + Doxycycline 100mg IV BID + Metronidazole 500mg PO BID (alternatives: Clindamycin+gentamicin, Ofloxacin+Metronidazole, Levofloxacin+Metronidazole, Amp/Sulbactam+Doxycycline, Cipro+Doxy+metronidazole); outpatient CTX 250mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14d +/- flagyl if BV; inpatient Cefotetan 2g IV q12h OR cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + doxycycline. Duration: 14 days if uncomplicated (up to 4-6 weeks for TOA). Uncomplicated treatment: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + Doxycycline x14d OR Cefoxitin 2g IM x1 + Probenecid 1g PO x1 + Doxycycline x14d (add flagyl given clue cells/BV)
